title: "Week 10: Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality, and Grid Computing"

## Week Overview

This week introduces Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Mixed Reality (MR), covering how each technology works, their hardware and software components, key features, major application areas, and the limitations and ethical concerns surrounding immersive technologies. It then introduces Grid Computing, its features, architecture, comparison with cluster and cloud computing, limitations, and application areas.

**Course Outcome:** CO 5  
**Duration:** 1 week

---

## Lecture 26: Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality {#lecture-26}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}

### Learning Objectives
- Define Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR)
- Distinguish AR, VR, and Mixed Reality (MR)
- Identify the hardware and software components of AR/VR systems
- Explain the main features of AR and VR
- Describe major application areas of AR and VR
- State the limitations and challenges of AR/VR technologies

### Topics Covered
- The reality-virtuality continuum and Extended Reality (XR)
- What is Augmented Reality, how it works, and its types (marker-based, markerless, location-based, projection-based, superimposition-based)
- What is Virtual Reality, its core concepts, and system architecture
- Hardware components (displays, sensors, input, processing, feedback, connectivity) and software components (3D modelling, game engines, AR SDKs, WebXR/OpenXR, computer vision, cloud services)
- AR vs VR comparison and Mixed Reality
- Applications in education, healthcare, industry, architecture, retail, defence, tourism, and entertainment
- Advantages, limitations, and privacy/ethical concerns of AR/VR
- Future trends in immersive technologies

### Key Concepts
- **AR**: Augmented Reality; digital content overlaid on the real world
- **VR**: Virtual Reality; fully computer-generated immersive environment
- **MR**: Mixed Reality; real and virtual objects interact
- **XR**: Extended Reality; umbrella term for AR, VR, and MR
- **HMD**: Head-Mounted Display
- **Immersion**: degree to which the system engages the user's senses
- **Presence**: feeling of being inside the virtual environment
- **DoF**: Degrees of Freedom of tracked movement
- **Latency**: delay between user action and system response
- **Registration**: alignment of virtual content with the real world

### Case Study
- Training a Surgeon with VR and AR: practicing procedures on a virtual patient (VR), building 3D models from CT/MRI scans for planning (VR/AR), overlaying key information during surgery (AR), and recording performance for feedback

### Key Takeaways

- AR overlays digital content on the real world; VR replaces the real world with a virtual one.
- MR lets real and virtual objects interact; XR covers AR, VR, and MR.
- AR works through capture, tracking, registration, rendering, and display.
- VR depends on tracking, processing, and display with low latency for immersion and presence.
- Both technologies are used in education, healthcare, industry, defence, retail, tourism, and entertainment.
- Cost, health effects, hardware limits, content creation, and privacy are major challenges.

## Lecture 27: Grid Computing {#lecture-27}

### Learning Objectives
- Define grid computing and explain why it is needed
- Describe the main features of a computing grid
- Explain the architecture and working of a grid
- Compare grid computing with cluster and cloud computing
- State the limitations and challenges of grid computing
- Identify major application areas of grid computing

### Topics Covered
- Need for grid computing and the electric power grid analogy
- Definition of grid computing and the divide, distribute, and combine idea
- Key features: resource sharing, heterogeneity, scalability, loose coupling, decentralised control, and reliability
- Types of grids: computational, data, collaborative, volunteer, and enterprise
- Grid architecture: application, middleware, resource, and fabric layers, and how a job runs on a grid
- Grid vs cluster computing and grid vs cloud computing
- Advantages, limitations, and challenges
- Application areas and well-known projects such as WLCG, SETI@home, Folding@home, and BOINC

### Key Concepts
- **Grid computing**: dispersed, heterogeneous resources working together as one virtual supercomputer
- **Node**: an individual computer or resource in the grid
- **Middleware**: software layer for resource discovery, scheduling, security, and monitoring
- **Scheduler**: assigns tasks to suitable nodes
- **Virtual organisation**: group of institutions sharing grid resources under agreed rules
- **Volunteer computing**: donating idle computer time to a project

### Case Study
- Analysing Particle-Physics Data: petabytes of experiment data are stored and processed across many computing centres worldwide so thousands of researchers can analyse it together

### Key Takeaways

- Grid computing links dispersed, heterogeneous computers into one virtual supercomputer.
- Its key features are resource sharing, scalability, heterogeneity, loose coupling, and decentralised control.
- A grid has application, middleware, resource, and fabric layers; middleware handles scheduling, security, and monitoring.
- A cluster is tightly coupled and local, a grid is loosely coupled and multi-organisational, and a cloud offers on-demand rented services.
- Major challenges are security, complex setup, network dependence, and unpredictable node availability.
- Grids are widely used in science, healthcare, engineering, finance, and weather forecasting.
